# Glossary — plain-language camera terms

For readers new to photography. Definitions are plain-language; where a line
states a factual spec it carries a citation, but pure definitions need none.
Back to the [README](README.md) or [full analysis](canon-mirrorless-system.md).

| Term | Plain meaning |
|------|---------------|
| **Mirrorless** | A camera with no flip-up mirror (unlike older DSLRs). Lighter and smaller, with a live electronic preview. Canon's mirrorless line is the "EOS R" series. |
| **RF mount** | The lens connection on Canon full-frame mirrorless bodies. Any "RF" lens fits any EOS R body. |
| **RF-S lens** | An RF-mount lens designed for Canon's smaller (APS-C) sensors. Cheaper and lighter, but only uses the full image circle on APS-C bodies. |
| **Sensor** | The chip that captures light. Bigger sensor = generally better low-light and more background blur, but bigger/heavier/pricier gear. |
| **Full-frame** | The larger sensor size (~36×24 mm). Best low-light, shallowest background blur. Bodies and lenses run heavier and cost more. |
| **APS-C** | A smaller sensor (~1.6× smaller each dimension on Canon). Lighter, cheaper bodies and lenses; slightly less low-light ability. |
| **Crop factor (1.6×)** | Because Canon APS-C is smaller, a lens "sees" a narrower, more zoomed-in view. Multiply the lens number by 1.6 to get the full-frame-equivalent view: a 50 mm lens looks like ~80 mm [[28]](citations.md#c28). |
| **Focal length (mm)** | How zoomed-in a lens is. Small numbers (16–35 mm) = wide views for landscapes; bigger numbers (85–135 mm) = zoomed-in, flattering for portraits. |
| **Wide / ultra-wide** | "Wide" fits a lot of scene in (good for landscapes). "Ultra-wide" (roughly under 24 mm equivalent) fits even more and exaggerates depth. |
| **Prime lens** | A lens with one fixed focal length (e.g. 50 mm). Usually lighter, sharper, and lets in more light than a zoom — but you "zoom with your feet." |
| **Zoom lens** | A lens covering a range (e.g. 24–105 mm). One lens does many jobs — convenient for travel — at some cost to size/sharpness/light. |
| **Aperture / f-number** | How wide the lens opens. **Lower number = wider opening = more light + more background blur.** f/1.8 is "fast/bright"; f/6.3 is "slow/dim." |
| **Bokeh** | The soft, blurry background a wide aperture produces — separates your subject from the scene. |
| **IS (Image Stabilization)** | Anti-shake built into a lens. Lets you shoot sharper at slower shutter speeds / lower light, handheld. |
| **IBIS (In-Body IS)** | Anti-shake built into the camera body, so it helps with any lens. Only some Canon bodies have it (e.g. R7, R6 II); cheaper bodies often don't [[4]](citations.md#c4)[[3]](citations.md#c3). |
| **Stops** | A unit of light/stabilization. "8 stops of IBIS" means much steadier handheld shots. Each stop doubles or halves the effect. |
| **Magnification ratio / 1:1** | How big a small subject lands on the sensor. **1:1 (life-size) = "true macro."** 0.5× = half life-size (good close-ups, not true macro) [[36]](citations.md#c36). |
| **Working distance** | The gap between the front of the lens and your subject when focused close. Longer is better for shy bugs and avoids casting shadows. |
| **Weather sealing** | Gaskets that resist dust and light rain. Useful for landscapes/travel; mostly on pricier "L" lenses and higher-end bodies. |
| **L-series** | Canon's professional lens line (red ring). Best optics + weather sealing, but heaviest and most expensive. |
| **Kit lens** | The basic zoom often bundled with a body (e.g. RF-S 18-45mm). Light and cheap; a fine starting point. |
| **Superzoom / all-in-one** | A zoom with a huge range (e.g. 18-150mm, 24-240mm). One-lens convenience; some image-quality compromise [[45]](citations.md#c45). |
| **CIPA weight** | The industry-standard way to state camera weight: body **with** battery and memory card. "Body-only" numbers are lighter and not comparable. |
| **Quick-release (QR) plate** | A small plate you attach to the camera once; it clicks onto the tripod so you don't screw the camera on each time. |
| **Lever clamp vs screw-knob** | Two ways a tripod holds the QR plate. A **lever** flips open/shut (easy on weak hands); a **screw-knob** twists (more grip effort) [[69]](citations.md#c69). |
| **Flip/lever leg lock vs twist lock** | Two ways tripod legs lock. **Flip/lever** = press a small lever (thumb-friendly). **Twist** = rotate a collar (needs grip/torque) [[79]](citations.md#c79). |
| **Arca-Swiss** | The most common QR plate "standard." Widely compatible, but not perfectly standardized between brands [[76]](citations.md#c76). |
| **Monopod** | A single-leg support. The camera leans on it so your hands don't bear all the weight — lighter than a tripod. |
| **VCM / USM / STM** | Types of lens autofocus motors. USM/VCM are faster and quieter (pricier lenses); STM is good and affordable (budget lenses). |
